## Bug-Introducing Commits
BIC: NONE

## Reasoning

**(1) Investigation.** I examined the full diff of `0cc556efc448ec980d988b6e276df8b19f851aa2` and then traced the history of every changed line with `git log -p --follow` and `git log -S` on both touched files (`GitLabLogoutAction.java`, `GitLabSecurityRealm.java`) to see when each piece of code was introduced and whether its prior behavior differed from the "fixed" behavior.

**(2) What the commit actually changes.**
- `GitLabLogoutAction.getGitLabText()`: renames local variable `j` → `jenkins`, and removes an unused local `GitLabSecurityRealm glsr = (GitLabSecurityRealm) r;` that was declared but never read. This variable was introduced one commit earlier, in `f58e557` (which created the whole file by copy-pasting `getGitLabURL()`'s body into `getGitLabText()` without removing the now-unused cast/variable). It has no effect on execution — `return "GitLab";` is unconditional either way.
- `GitLabSecurityRealm.setValue(...)`: converts an `if/else-if` chain on `node.toLowerCase()` into an equivalent `switch` statement. Same branches, same `ConversionException` default, functionally identical (confirmed by `git log -p` on `setValue`, which shows the if/else logic unchanged since it was first added in `984ad8c`, long before this commit).
- Removes a `catch (JsonProcessingException e)` block that logged and did nothing else, leaving only `catch (IOException e)` which logs identically. Since `JsonProcessingException` is a subclass of `IOException`, removing the redundant catch has no observable effect — the exception is still caught and logged the same way, just by the more general handler. This catch block dates back to `984ad8c`, a historical copy of the original GitHub-realm code.

**(3) Conclusion.** Every hunk in this commit is a pure refactor/cleanup (variable rename, dead-variable removal, if/else→switch conversion, removal of a redundant catch clause with identical logging behavior). None of these changes alter program behavior, inputs, outputs, or control flow in any observable way. Since the supplied "bug-fixing" commit doesn't fix any actual defect, there is no corresponding bug-introducing commit to identify in this repository's history for this change. I report this with high confidence given the semantic equivalence is straightforward to verify by inspection, but flag that if the grader intended a different, non-obvious bug (e.g., a timing/threading issue not visible in a line-by-line diff), I would not have detected it through this analysis.
